protocol.name: wc_clipboard_v1

description.summary: the system clipboard as bytes, for a client that cannot be handed a pipe

protocol.description:
wl_data_offer.receive hands the compositor a **file descriptor** and asks it to write the selection into it. wl_data_source.send does the mirror image. Both are unimplementable across this project's boundary, and not because they are hard: docs/waycompose-design.md §2.1 forbids a descriptor crossing at all, and a pipe is the one kind of shared object that cannot be replaced by a name — a name can be opened by the far side, a pipe's *other end* cannot be conjured from one.
So the transfer is terminated where the descriptor is real. wc-proxy runs on the same machine as the Wayland client, keeps the client's fd, and speaks this interface to the compositor instead. Nothing here is a descriptor; everything is an array or a string.
That is the same trade wc_icon_manager_v1 made for icon pixels (§16.5), for the same reason and with the same chunking limit: wayland-backend's buffers are 4096 bytes in both directions, so a payload of any size has to arrive in pieces.
**This interface does not announce anything.** Which client may see the selection, and when, is wl_data_device's business and smithay's; the compositor sets a normal compositor-provided selection from whatever the Win32 clipboard holds and the offers reach the client over the ordinary protocol, proxied verbatim. This interface carries only the two things that would otherwise need a pipe: the bytes out, and the bytes back.

interface.name: wc_clipboard_manager_v1

description.summary: publishes and fetches the system clipboard's contents

interface.description:
A publisher builds one selection out of band and then installs it: chunk* data, repeated once per mime type, and finally publish. A reader asks for one mime type with fetch and is answered with chunk* done, or with fail.
Requests and events are matched by a **token** chosen by the client rather than by object, because a fetch is not an object and minting one per paste would put a round trip in front of every one. Tokens are the client's to reuse once done or fail has arrived for them.

entry.name: too_big
entry.summary: more staged bytes than the compositor will hold

entry.name: too_many
entry.summary: more mime types in one selection than the compositor will hold

request.name: destroy
request.description:
Whatever was published stays on the system clipboard. Destroying this object does not take it back, for the same reason closing a Windows application does not empty the clipboard.
Fetches still outstanding are abandoned; no done or fail will arrive for them.

request.name: chunk

description.summary: append bytes to the staging area

request.description: The bytes are the payload for the mime type the next data request will name, in whatever encoding that mime type implies. Send as many chunks as it takes; the split points carry no meaning.

arg.name: data
arg.summary: a piece of the next payload

request.name: data

description.summary: close off the payload for one mime type

request.description: Takes everything staged so far as the contents for this mime type and empties the staging area. A mime type named twice in one selection replaces the earlier payload.

request.name: publish

description.summary: install the staged selection as the system clipboard

request.description:
Replaces the clipboard's entire contents. Publishing with nothing staged empties it, which is what a client clearing its selection (wl_data_device.set_selection with a null source) means.
Mime types the compositor has no system format for are dropped rather than refused: a Wayland client offers everything it can produce and a clipboard holds what the system knows how to hold, so a selection offering fifteen flavours of text and one image is a success even if only two of them survive.

request.name: start_drag

description.summary: begin a system drag carrying the staged selection

request.description:
Takes the staged set exactly as publish does — same chunk, same data, same staging area — and hands it to the system's own drag and drop instead of to the clipboard. On Windows that is DoDragDrop with an IDataObject built from the same formats a publish would have set.
**The payload is staged before the drag starts, and that is forced rather than chosen.** OLE asks the drag source for the bytes with a synchronous IDataObject::GetData call from inside a modal loop; there is no round trip available to a Wayland client on another machine at that moment. So a drag costs the same eager read a copy does, which is the same read, in the same place, through the same code.
Ends with drag_finished, always: a drop, a cancellation and a failure to start are all answered.

request.name: cancel_drag
request.description: A Wayland client that destroys its data source mid-drag means this. If no drag is running it is ignored.

enum.name: source

description.summary: which system selection a fetch is asking about

enum.description: Two, because Windows keeps them apart: the clipboard is a global that outlives every window, and a drag's data belongs to one gesture and is gone when it ends. Asking the wrong one is how a paste picks up the last thing dragged.

entry.name: drag
entry.summary: the drag currently over one of this compositor's windows

request.name: fetch

description.summary: ask for the system clipboard, or the current drag, in one mime type

request.description:
Answered with chunk* done, or with fail if the source holds nothing convertible to this mime type.
**The answer is the clipboard as it is now, not as it was when the offer was made.** There is no serial and no snapshot: Windows' clipboard has one current owner and asking it is the only way to read it, so a user who copies again between the offer and the paste pastes the newer thing. X11 behaves the same way for the same reason.
A drag's data does not have that problem, because the compositor reads the whole IDataObject at the drop and answers out of that copy.

arg.name: source
arg.summary: a value from the source enum

event.name: chunk

description.summary: a piece of a fetched payload

event.description: Pieces arrive in order and are concatenated. An empty payload is zero chunks followed by done, which is not the same as fail: the clipboard can legitimately hold an empty string.

event.name: fail
event.description: The clipboard does not hold this mime type, or could not be opened. The reason is for a log, not for a client to match on.

event.name: drag_finished

description.summary: a drag started with start_drag has ended

event.description:
The action is what the drop target actually did, as a wl_data_device_manager.dnd_action value: none means the drag was cancelled or refused, and anything else means a drop happened and the source should tell its client so.
Exactly one of these arrives per start_drag.
